analysis.one_liner: Bars the EPA from issuing greenhouse gas rules until China, India, and Russia match U.S. Paris targets.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote; it was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in April 2021 and stayed there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop the Environmental Protection Agency from issuing any rule or regulation limiting greenhouse gas emissions until its Administrator determined that China, India, and Russia were each meeting the same emission-reduction targets the United States has under the Paris Agreement. Because those countries never committed to identical targets, the effect would have been an indefinite freeze on federal climate rules. The bill received a Senate introduction and referral to committee but no hearing, no vote, and no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be fossil fuel producers, power plants, and other emissions-intensive businesses that would avoid federal limits on greenhouse gases. The bill's stated rationale is protecting domestic manufacturers from costs that foreign competitors would not face.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the EPA Administrator from issuing any rule or regulation that regulates greenhouse gas emissions, overriding other provisions of law ([S3]).

Ties the freeze to a determination that China, India, and Russia each adhere to the same emission-reduction targets as the United States under the Paris Agreement, plus an annual certification afterward ([S3]).
The bill's title and stated purpose frame the freeze as protection for domestic manufacturing from countries that have not adopted the same targets ([S2], [S3]).

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall on the public: people exposed to air pollution and the effects of a changing climate, since federal greenhouse gas limits would be suspended indefinitely, and on state and local governments and businesses that had planned around EPA climate rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone exposed to pollution and climate costs

drawbacks.text: The condition for lifting the ban is one no foreign country has met; China, India, and Russia have not adopted the same emission-reduction targets as the United States, so the bill is written as a permanent bar on EPA climate rules rather than a temporary one ([S2], [S3]).

Suspending federal greenhouse gas regulation would leave U.S. emissions unchecked regardless of what other countries do, abandoning the reductions the United States committed to under the Paris Agreement ([S2], [S3]).

The strongest good-faith objection supporters would acknowledge in reverse: U.S. climate rules can impose compliance costs on manufacturers while emissions in China, India, and Russia keep growing, which the bill's framing as 'Domestic Manufacturing Protection' reflects ([S3]).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades an indefinite suspension of federal climate regulation for a condition (identical targets from China, India, and Russia) that has not been met, so the practical effect is a one-sided freeze. Whatever relief it offers manufacturers on compliance costs, the public pays in unchecked emissions, with no mechanism forcing the named countries to act.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Inhofe introduced the bill on April 22, 2021, with three Republican cosponsors (Tillis, Hyde-Smith, and Lankford) ([S3], [S4]).
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day ([S1], [S5]).
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended ([S5]).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, EPA kept its authority to issue greenhouse gas rules and the status quo on climate regulation held. The industries the bill would have shielded gained nothing beyond avoiding a vote they were not positioned to win.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Anyone counting on EPA climate rules

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oklahoma; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill prohibiting EPA greenhouse gas rules until China, India, and Russia meet U.S. Paris targets.

against.name: Sen. Tom Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill; it received no hearing or markup after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat or independent supported the bill; no Democratic chamber or committee action followed.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel producers and emissions-intensive manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have suspended all federal limits on their greenhouse gas emissions indefinitely, cutting compliance costs while leaving the pollution costs with the public. Its framing as protection for domestic manufacturing rests on the claim that foreign competitors face no comparable limits.
A freeze on EPA greenhouse gas rules would have removed the regulatory pressure that drives demand for cleaner power and equipment, slowing the shift these industries sell.
